patient.chief_complaint: Brought in by paramedics found on street unresponsive, pupils dilated, hyperthermia, intermittent rhythmic limb movements — suspected overdose vs SE
patient.history_present_illness: A 29-year-old Asian male graduate student was found unresponsive on a university campus sidewalk by a passerby who called 911. EMS found him supine, unresponsive, temperature 40.8°C (rectal), heart rate 156, blood pressure 94/56, diaphoretic, pupils 7 mm bilaterally and unreactive. Rhythmic twitching of the left arm was noted by EMS. He had no identification initially (student ID found later). His phone had an emergency contact who identified him as a 29-year-old neuroscience graduate student who was aware his experiments involved handling of organophosphate compounds for research. The contact did not know of any drugs of abuse. A search of his backpack yielded an open container of a known organophosphate compound used in his neurophysiology laboratory. In the ED he continues with mydriasis (7mm), hyperthermia 40.6°C, tachycardia 158, intermittent left arm and bilateral leg rhythmic movements, hypersalivation, and secretions requiring suction every few minutes. He is not responsive. The electroencephalographer reviewing the EEG notes 'continuous low-voltage beta activity possibly from drug effect or ictal activity.'

social_history.note: Graduate student, lives in university dorms. Researches organophosphate compounds in neurophysiology lab. No known drug use per emergency contact. International student from China.

neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 3 — unresponsive. No eye opening to pain. No verbal response. No motor response to commands. Profoundly comatose.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 7 mm bilaterally, round, unreactive to light (mydriasis). Corneal reflexes present bilaterally. Oculocephalic reflex present. No gag reflex elicited.
neurological_exam.motor: Intermittent rhythmic twitching of the left arm and bilateral legs. No purposeful movement. Diffuse hypotonia between ictal movements. No localising movements.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Symmetrically reduced deep tendon reflexes bilaterally. Bilateral plantar responses extensor.
neurological_exam.additional: Copious oral secretions requiring continuous suction. Diaphoretic, skin warm and flushed. Mydriasis, hyperthermia, tachycardia, hypotension, and secretions noted.

contraindications: Phenytoin: INEFFECTIVE for organophosphate-induced seizures — targets sodium channels not the acetylcholine excess mechanism; randomised trial data (COMBAT-OP) confirm no benefit; do not use.
Succinylcholine for RSI intubation: pseudocholinesterase critically inhibited in organophosphate poisoning — succinylcholine paralysis will be markedly prolonged (hours); use rocuronium exclusively.
warnings: Pralidoxime efficacy is time-dependent — enzyme aging (permanent phosphorylation of acetylcholinesterase) reduces efficacy with delayed administration.
Atropine clinical endpoint is typically drying of secretions; tachycardia alone is not a dose-limiting endpoint in organophosphate poisoning.

results.title: Acute organophosphate poisoning: clinical features, electrophysiology, and outcomes
results.key_finding: Organophosphate poisoning produces a cholinergic toxidrome through acetylcholinesterase inhibition. Electrophysiological features include generalized fast EEG patterns, neuromuscular junction dysfunction on repetitive nerve stimulation, and, in some patients, seizures. The intermediate syndrome — characterized by neuromuscular junction dysfunction and respiratory muscle weakness at 24–96 hours post-exposure — has been described in cohort studies. Comparative data on antidote regimens and antiseizure medication efficacy in this population are available in the literature.

output.summary: Published evidence on acute organophosphate poisoning documents the clinical and electrophysiological features of cholinergic toxidrome, the time-dependence of cholinesterase reactivation, the epidemiology of the intermediate syndrome, and comparative antiseizure medication efficacy data from randomized trials in this population. Succinylcholine pharmacokinetics are described in the context of pseudocholinesterase inhibition.

Negative inspiratory force (NIF): -22 cmH2O (normal < -25 cmH2O) — borderline respiratory muscle weakness.

The electrophysiological pattern is consistent with neuromuscular junction dysfunction

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
No structural workup needed acutely — tox cause clear; MRI may be considered later if encephalopathy persists.

sequence_constraints.reason: Cholinesterase level confirms OP etiology before pralidoxime; do not delay empiric treatment if strongly suspected.

critical_actions: Atropine IV titrated to bronchial secretion control — large doses often needed
Pralidoxime 1-2 g IV early — before enzyme aging (typically <24h)
Mechanical ventilation; do NOT use succinylcholine for intubation
Anticipate intermediate syndrome at 24-96h — prolonged ventilation
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT use succinylcholine — prolonged paralysis from cholinesterase inhibition
Do NOT use morphine — worsens respiratory depression
Do NOT extubate prematurely — intermediate syndrome can cause delayed respiratory failure
Do NOT use phenytoin as first-line — benzodiazepines are first-line in OP seizures
Do NOT use succinylcholine for paralysis in OP poisoning — prolonged paralysis due to pseudocholinesterase inhibition.
Avoid morphine and other agents that can worsen bronchorrhea and respiratory depression in cholinergic crisis.
key_reasoning_points: Cholinergic toxidrome (DUMBELS: diarrhea, urination, miosis, bronchorrhea/bronchospasm, emesis, lacrimation, salivation) + nicotinic features (fasciculation, weakness, tachycardia, hypertension)
Pralidoxime must be given early before enzyme aging (24-48h for most OPs)
Intermediate syndrome at 24-96h causes delayed respiratory failure requiring continued ventilation
Succinylcholine is contraindicated — pseudocholinesterase inhibition causes prolonged paralysis

Routine tox screens do NOT include organophosphates; specific cholinesterase levels are required
